newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court hears two redistricting cases.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court hears two redistricting cases.

text.p: The Supreme Court heard arguments Monday in a pair of redistricting cases involving the drawing of boundaries under the federal voting rights law to enhance the voting strength of blacks.

In one case the Justice Department and an American Civil Liberties Union attorney asked the high court to overturn a ruling that eliminated two of Georgia's three congressional districts containing a majority of black voters.
They said there should be at least two districts in the state with a majority of black voters, a position Georgia's attorney general opposed.

In the other case the justices considered a Louisiana school board redistricting plan. The case involves the standard the Justice Department should apply in deciding whether to approve changes in boundary lines.
In the Georgia case the Supreme Court in 1995 struck down an earlier redistricting plan, saying it was unconstitutional to draw congressional districts based mainly on race.
The state legislature then could not agree on a new electoral map and a federal, three-judge panel rearranged seven of Georgia's 11 congressional districts.
The court-imposed plan, used in the November election, has just one district with a majority of black voters and six with black populations ranging from 23 percent to 35 percent.

Deputy Solicitor General Seth Waxman said the judges should have adopted the Justice Department's proposal calling for two majority black districts, even though it would have split up Bibb and Muscogee counties.
American Civil Liberties Union lawyer Laughlin McDonald urged the justices to overturn the lower-court ruling and send the case back for a new plan with two majority black districts.

Georgia Attorney General Michael Bowers said there was no evidence a second majority black district was required. He asked the court to uphold the ruling, giving states and judges more discretion in drawing boundaries.

Lee Parks, an attorney representing white voters, called the judicially imposed redistricting a "caretaker plan," with the state legislature free to change it during its next session or after the 2000 census.
The Supreme Court took both cases under advisement, with decisions due before the end of its 1996-97 term in June.
